

**TrafficEye: An Integrated Crowdsourced and AI-Assisted System for Traffic Violation Reporting and Enforcement**

Meenakshi Garg1, Shivam Chauhan2, Mohit Jain3, Aditya Jaiswar4

Vivekanand Education Society’s Institute of Technology, Mumbai-400074, India

## **Abstract**

Citizen traffic-violation reports can extend enforcement coverage, but interpreting submitted evidence places a substantial burden on reporters and reviewing officers. TrafficEye addresses this problem by combining mobile evidence collection with AI-assisted visual triage. The prototype uses a cross-platform mobile framework for the client, a managed backend-as-a-service platform with a relational database for storage and synchronization, GPS and EXIF metadata for geolocation, and a pretrained Vision-Language Model (VLM) for visual inference. It organizes vehicle descriptions, candidate violations, license-plate strings, and severity labels into reports for officer verification. The principal outcome is an integrated citizen-to-officer workflow; domain-specific accuracy and operational benefits have not yet been quantitatively evaluated. A planned evaluation covers classification, vehicle detection, plate recognition, and severity agreement. The work contributes a system integration approach whose effectiveness requires application-level validation.

***Keywords:** Traffic Violation Detection · Crowdsourced Traffic Reporting · Vision-Language Model (VLM) Multimodal Visual Inference · Automatic Number Plate Recognition · Geolocation · Human-in-the-Loop Review*

# **1\. Introduction**

Fixed surveillance cameras and localized police patrols leave gaps in urban traffic-enforcement coverage. Smartphone-based crowdsourcing offers a complementary means of collecting road-safety information from everyday road users \[1–4\]. Such participation can help document violations and dangerous road conditions \[2–5\], while platforms such as Delhi Traffic Prahari already accept citizen photographs and videos for police verification \[6\]. However, evidence collection alone does not resolve the work of identifying vehicles, interpreting violations, transcribing plates, and deciding which reports require attention.

Dedicated plate-recognition and helmet-violation pipelines address these interpretation tasks, but their development generally requires task-specific data and models \[7–10\]. TrafficEye integrates citizen reporting with a pretrained Vision-Language Model (VLM) to assist officer review. The objective is to organize evidence and candidate interpretations without developing a custom-trained vision model. The contribution is system-level integration; its accuracy and operational benefits require evaluation.

# **2\. Related Work / Literature Review**

Crowdsourced enforcement systems address the collection and handling of reports before an authority decides whether action is warranted. RoadCop, proposed by Jameela et al., uses a bi-modular design in which citizen video submissions undergo an initial spam-filtering stage followed by evaluation for enforcement \[1\]. Its relevance to TrafficEye lies in separating incoming reports from accepted evidence. Screening submission quality, however, is a different task from extracting a plate string or assigning a candidate violation category. This distinction motivates retaining a review stage even when visual interpretation is assisted by AI.

Aubry et al. developed CrowdOut to support real-time offence reporting and visualization on a city map \[2\]. Mobile Roadwatch, described by KAIST, combines smartphone video capture with automatic location and time tagging, allowing users to select events for police reporting \[12\]. Together, these approaches connect an observed event to media and spatial context. They inform TrafficEye’s capture-and-location workflow, but their documented reporting functions do not by themselves establish automated plate recognition or severity assessment. Map-based presentation and metadata capture address where an event occurred; interpreting its evidentiary meaning remains a separate concern.

Related work broadens the role of citizen input beyond individual offences. Olma et al. examine road users’ reports of danger spots, while Dunlop et al. investigate smartphone contributions to identifying dangerous road sections and providing warnings \[3, 4\]. These studies support the use of distributed road-user observations as a source of safety information. Their emphasis also clarifies an application boundary: identifying a hazardous location and preparing an individual violation report serve different purposes. TrafficEye uses citizen evidence for the latter and must therefore associate the media, location, vehicle, and review decision within each submission.

In India, Traffic Prahari accepts photographs or videos together with the event’s date, time, location, registration number, and violation type, followed by traffic-police verification \[6\]. The Mumbai Traffic Police application also provides citizen violation-reporting channels \[13\]. These services establish a practical reporting-to-authority workflow in which users supply details and police review the evidence. Automated vision analysis and real-time backend behavior are not established by the cited descriptions; undocumented features should not be treated as proven absences. TrafficEye builds on the same human-review model while proposing AI-generated fields to assist initial interpretation.

Task-specific computer vision provides a different route to reducing interpretation effort. Srivastava et al. combine YOLOv5 plate detection with EasyOCR character recognition for Indian vehicles \[7\], whereas Deshpande et al. develop a two-stage pipeline for two-wheeler helmet-violation detection and vehicle identification in Indian traffic \[8\]. These approaches target clearly defined visual tasks and provide reference points for evaluating plate extraction and violation analysis separately. Their specialized pipelines also illustrate the development work associated with supporting multiple enforcement tasks. TrafficEye adopts API-based inference to avoid building and maintaining its own labeled training data and detector, while accepting less task-specific control.

The license-plate recognition surveys by Shashirangana et al. and Xu et al. place such pipelines within a broader combination of detection, recognition, OCR, and image-processing methods \[9, 10\]. Lighting, viewpoint, weather, plate visibility, and dataset characteristics affect how performance should be interpreted. For TrafficEye, these observations mean that producing a plausible plate string is insufficient evidence of reliable recognition. The planned evaluation consequently distinguishes exact plate matches from character-level accuracy and includes adverse capture conditions. Dedicated ANPR research provides evaluation context, not accuracy figures transferable to TrafficEye.

Vision-language research motivates using a reusable inference component across related visual tasks. Zhang et al. review visual recognition using models that connect image and language representations \[15\], and Caffagni et al. examine multimodal models, their capabilities, datasets, and evaluation benchmarks \[16\]. The VLM’s image-understanding API supports the visual inference used by TrafficEye \[14\]. These sources support the choice of a pretrained multimodal inference layer, but they do not validate this application’s traffic classifications. Whether one prompted model can consistently supply vehicle, violation, plate, and severity fields remains an application-level evaluation question.

Adoption introduces constraints beyond recognition performance. Khojastehpour et al. identify privacy concerns, perceived penalty fairness, and trust in police performance as influences on acceptance of crowdsourced enforcement \[5\]. Dasgupta et al. emphasize human involvement and accountability in AI-assisted law enforcement \[11\]. These findings inform TrafficEye’s officer-verification step and the need for future bystander anonymization. A severity label can help organize a queue, but it does not remove the reviewing authority’s responsibility to examine the original evidence. Privacy and fairness therefore remain design considerations alongside the technical reporting pipeline.

Across the reviewed work, evidence collection, location context, visual interpretation, and accountable review are addressed with different emphases \[1–5, 7–9, 12\]. The gap addressed here is their integration within one citizen-to-officer workflow using GPS/EXIF handling and pretrained visual inference. TrafficEye combines structured analysis with managed cloud object storage, a relational database, and real-time synchronization, while retaining officer decisions. Comparative performance remains to be established through empirical evaluation.

# **3\. Problem Statement**

TrafficEye addresses five connected operational problems:

- **Limited enforcement coverage:** fixed cameras and patrol teams cannot continuously observe every road or junction.
- **Inconsistent citizen evidence:** submitted photographs and videos differ in clarity, viewpoint, lighting, and completeness.
- **Time-consuming manual triage:** officers must repeatedly identify vehicles, interpret possible violations, and transcribe registration plates before a case can be reviewed.
- **Uncertain location metadata:** GPS and EXIF data provide useful context, but may be missing, altered, or insufficient as independent proof.
- **Need for accountable automation:** AI can assist with preliminary interpretation, but enforcement decisions must remain with an authorized officer.

The problem is therefore to create a single reporting workflow that captures evidence, records available location context, prepares structured candidate fields, and supports officer verification without treating model output as a final decision.

# **4\. Proposed TrafficEye System and Methodology**

TrafficEye follows a “Capture – Verify – Submit” interaction. A citizen captures photographic or video evidence, or selects existing media, checks the detected location and pre-filled details, and submits the report. The aim is to keep reporting brief, consistent with smartphone-based road-safety participation \[3, 4\]. Submitted evidence receives candidate analysis fields before entering the officer queue. Officers inspect the original media and may confirm, edit, or reject a report; the citizen’s submission status is then updated. This human-in-the-loop review preserves officer oversight within the enforcement-support process \[11\].

Quantitative evaluation is planned and has not yet been conducted. The protocol targets approximately 50–100 traffic images and short clips covering supported categories, such as no-helmet, red-light, and wrong-parking violations. It includes favorable conditions and difficult cases involving low light, oblique viewpoints, or partially occluded plates. This collection is an evaluation set, not a training dataset. Application-specific testing is necessary because general multimodal benchmarks do not establish performance for the reporting workflow \[15, 16\].

The three project members will independently label vehicle presence, violation category, the correct plate string, and a subjective severity label for each item. They will resolve disagreements by consensus to establish reference labels. The same items will then pass through TrafficEye with the model and prompting configuration held unchanged across test items. Recorded outputs will be assessed using violation-classification accuracy, vehicle-detection recall, plate exact-match and character-level OCR accuracy, and agreement with the reference severity labels. No model training or fine-tuning forms part of this protocol.

# **5\. System Architecture**

The architecture links a Citizen Reporting Interface and a Traffic Officer Command Center through a shared managed cloud backend. Figure 1 shows the relationships among media capture, location metadata, cloud storage, VLM inference, and structured reports. The backend stores submissions and supports real-time synchronization with the officer interface. The inference component supplies candidate vehicle descriptions, violations, plate strings, and severity labels from the submitted evidence \[14–16\].

Fig. 1\. TrafficEye system architecture: citizen capture, cloud backend, VLM inference, and officer review.

Evidence and metadata move from the client to the backend for storage and API-based analysis. Parsed outputs are assembled into a report and presented with the original evidence in the officer verification queue. The arrows in Figure 1 distinguish the storage and analysis paths feeding review. Severity labels support prioritization; officers retain the decision to confirm, correct, or reject a submission. Review decisions are reflected in the shared report status, connecting the officer’s action back to the citizen-facing workflow.

# **6\. Implementation**

The mobile client uses a cross-platform mobile development framework for a shared Android/iOS codebase. Its managed toolchain provides camera, GPS, and local-storage access, and the interface uses a navy-and-amber theme. For a live photo, the application obtains latitude and longitude from the device. For gallery images, it reads available EXIF geotags, capture time, and device information, then compares the recorded location with the user’s current position as a plausibility check. EXIF can be edited or stripped, so this check does not provide tamper-proof location verification.

The backend platform supplies object storage for submitted media, a managed relational database for report data, and subscriptions that bring new reports into the officer interface without manual refresh. The report data links the evidence and location metadata with analysis fields and submission status. The database design supports querying by status, location, and severity. Concurrent submission handling is a design objective; backend throughput and scalability have not been validated by formal load testing. Network access is required for media upload and remote inference, so poor connectivity can interrupt submissions.

Before inference, the processing workflow compresses the evidence and normalizes its format. The implementation accesses its pretrained VLM through a hosted multimodal inference API, submitting images or video frames with a task-specific prompt requesting structured output. The returned response is parsed into vehicle description, candidate violation category, plate string, and severity fields \[14–16\]. Plate extraction is obtained from the same response or a follow-up inference call. Severity uses a small fixed category set, exemplified by Low, Medium, High, and Critical. Figure 2 shows the conceptual sequence from submission through preprocessing, interpretation, report assembly, and officer review.

*Fig. 2\. Conceptual VLM inference pipeline used by TrafficEye (inference only; no training/fine-tuning).*

The AI component performs inference only: TrafficEye does not train, fine-tune, or modify the pretrained model, and the project has no model-training dataset or train/validation/test split. This avoids a dedicated training pipeline, while giving the application less control than task-specific approaches such as those in \[7, 8\]. After parsing, the structured report and original media become available to officers for verification. Their confirmation, corrections, or rejection update the report status. The workflow is intended to reduce initial categorization and data entry, although its effects on review time and reporting completion have not yet been measured.

# **7\. Results and Discussion**

The current outcome is a prototype that integrates citizen evidence capture, GPS/EXIF location handling, cloud synchronization, and AI-assisted report preparation for officer review. Domain-specific quantitative evaluation remains pending, so classification accuracy, vehicle-detection recall, plate-recognition accuracy, and severity agreement cannot yet be reported. General multimodal-model benchmarks cannot substitute for the planned application-level measurements \[15, 16\]. The workflow provides a basis for examining whether structured candidate fields reduce manual triage, but no measured improvement in review speed or user satisfaction has been established. Low light, heavy rain, and obscured or damaged plates remain relevant reliability concerns \[10, 15, 16\]. Editable location metadata, connectivity dependence, and the absence of automatic bystander anonymization also limit the present prototype. These constraints support retaining officer verification and treating privacy, fairness, and trust as part of subsequent evaluation \[5, 11\]. Figures 3 and 4 illustrate the prototype interface: the officer pending-review queue and the AI-assisted verification screen, respectively.

# **8\. Conclusion and Future Scope**

TrafficEye combines mobile crowdsourcing, location metadata, cloud services, and pretrained visual inference within a citizen-to-officer traffic-reporting workflow. Its main contribution is the integration of these components with human verification rather than the introduction of a new detection algorithm. The prototype demonstrates a practical reporting and review process, although its accuracy and operational value still require formal evaluation. The immediate priority is to conduct the planned domain-specific study and examine plate-recognition performance across varied lighting, viewpoints, and levels of occlusion.

Further development can add officer filtering by assigned precinct or a configurable radius, and a city-wide heatmap to support patrol planning. Other priorities include bystander and non-violating-vehicle anonymization, backend load testing, and stronger location checks combining EXIF with additional signals. A proposed location-confidence score would require independent validation before any evidentiary claims. In the longer term, officer-verified reports could support registration lookup, evidence-linked digital challans, and vehicle-owner notification through an authorized RTO/DMV integration. These extensions remain planned work and have not been implemented or evaluated.
